`DELETE /archives` (issue #63), body `{ids: [...]}` — same "plural resource, `DELETE` with a
JSON body carrying which ones" shape `activity.rs::bulk_delete_activity` (`DELETE /activity`)
already established in this codebase, not a `POST .../batch-delete` action-style path; `DELETE`
*can* carry a request body per RFC 9110 (silently dropped by some older proxies/clients in
practice, but Axum and this project's own frontend both handle it fine, and precedent already
exists here). The Batch page's own "delete archives" operation previously fired
`DELETE /archives/{id}` once per selected archive from the frontend as a plain sequential loop
(no atomicity, no single audit point, and — since each request only ever reported its own
pass/fail — no way for the caller to know *which* ids failed without diffing the library
before/after). This does the same per-id work (`delete_one_archive`, identical cleanup to the
single-delete endpoint) server-side in one request, and reports a per-id result list so the
frontend can show exactly what happened rather than assuming full success.

Session-only (`route_policy.csv` denies every token role and `anonymous`) — deliberately
stricter than every other archive-mutating endpoint in this file, all of which a Token (Admin
or Guest) can call. A single wrong/leaked API token being able to wipe an arbitrary-sized slice
of the library in one request is a materially larger blast radius than any one of the
single-target endpoints token access already permits, and this project has no legitimate
automation use case for bulk deletion the way it does for e.g. scripted uploads or metadata
edits — so the extra restriction has no real workflow it breaks.

post.description:
Creates a session (an empty staged file plus a sidecar describing it) and returns the id. If
`client_key` matches a session that is still alive, that session is returned instead, with the
offset its bytes are already at — which is what makes a page refresh resumable rather than
restarting the transfer.

The returned `offset` is always read from the staged file's real length, never from the
sidecar, so a truncated or edited sidecar cannot make the server believe it holds bytes it
does not.

Sessions that have not been touched for 24 hours are swept by the operations here; the staged
bytes also live in `temp_dir`, so `DELETE /api/tempfolder` reclaims them too.

200.description: A session to upload into.

post.summary: Start or re-attach to a resumable upload

delete.description: Drops the staged bytes and the sidecar. Safe to call on an unknown id.

200.description: The session's bytes are gone (whether or not it existed).

get.description: The handshake a resuming client starts from: how many bytes the server actually holds for this session. `404` means unknown, expired, or already completed — in every case the client's correct move is to start a new session.

200.description: The session, with its current offset.

put.description:
Appends the request body to the staged file, but only at the position the client claims.
`Upload-Offset` is required and must equal the staged file's real length; the response always
reports the authoritative offset, including on failure:

- `204` — the chunk was appended; `Upload-Offset` is the new length.
- `409` — the client's offset disagrees with the disk (a lost response, a retried chunk, two
  tabs); `Upload-Offset` says where to resume from.
- `400` — missing or malformed `Upload-Offset`.

A connection that dies mid-chunk keeps whatever bytes reached the disk and reports the offset,
so a partial chunk is just fewer bytes rather than a corrupt one. The body is bounded at 64
MiB (the one-shot route is deliberately unbounded; a chunk is supposed to be small).

parameters.description: Byte position this chunk starts at; must equal the server's own length.
parameters.name: Upload-Offset

409.description: Offset mismatch; resync from the returned `Upload-Offset`.

post.description:
Verifies what landed, hashes it, and hands it to the same ingest the one-shot route uses —
including the persistent download-queue row, so a completed upload shows up (and can be
removed) exactly like any other queue item.

Verification: a `file_size` announced at session creation must equal the staged length
(`417` otherwise, and the staged bytes are dropped), and an optional `file_checksum` is
compared against the SHA-1 of the finished file (`417` on mismatch). That SHA-1 is computed by
reading the staged file once at this point rather than persisting incremental hasher state:
a resumed upload's early chunks were hashed by processes that are long gone, and state that
can silently desync from the bytes on disk is a worse trade than one sequential read of an
already-local file.

After this call the session no longer exists.

200.description: Ingested; the same body the one-shot upload returns.

417.description: The announced size or the supplied checksum did not match what arrived.

above, per issue #77's own confirmed two-phase design (see
`lanrurugi_imgcompare::compare_archives_streaming`'s own docs for the full phase-1/phase-2
breakdown): opens an `EventSource`-compatible stream (GET, not POST — `EventSource` can't send
a request body or use any other HTTP method) that emits one `event: sample` per
`CompareEvent::Sample` (coarse first, precise replacements streamed in afterward) and a single
terminal `event: done` carrying the rest of `ComparisonResult`'s own fields — never relies on

its result view the moment the FIRST `sample` event arrives rather than waiting for the whole
comparison, which for a ~200-page archive pair is otherwise several seconds of dead time
("假设有6对结果（粗加工），可以用sse分6次发，发第一对的时候就开始显示modal，这样是一个很大的提速").

A cache hit (same policy as `compare_queue_item`'s own) is replayed as a single burst of
`sample` events (`phase: coarse` for all of them — a cached result has already gone through
both phases, and the frontend only cares about "is this a display-final value", which `Coarse`
vs `Precise` doesn't actually change once the value itself is final) immediately followed by
`done`, so re-opening an already-computed comparison is still effectively instant.

Now that refresh tokens are stateful (`lanrurugi_storage::refresh_tokens`), logout actually
revokes — burns the entire refresh-token family the caller's access token was minted from
(same remediation `rotate`'s own reuse-detection path takes), not just clearing the browser's
cookies and hoping the now-orphaned access token quietly expires on its own within the next
few hours.

Reads `fid` out of the *access* token (`session::COOKIE_NAME`, `Path=/`), not the refresh
cookie — deliberately, so `REFRESH_COOKIE_PATH` can stay scoped to only
`POST /api/token/refresh` without also needing to cover this endpoint. Uses
`family_id_ignoring_expiry` rather than the normal expiry-checking verifier: a user who clicks
"log out" after their access token has already expired (idle tab, hasn't hit any endpoint that
would have triggered a silent refresh yet) must still get their refresh-token family actually
revoked — an already-expired access token still proves genuine origin via its signature, which
is all this needs.

A drill-down: given one bucket of one `/stats` chart, the archives in it, for the list the page
shows under the chart. Fetched per click rather than folded into `/stats/overview`, which is a
whole-library snapshot that would have to carry every bucket's archive list to support this.

Deliberately not expressed as a search query, even though some of these buckets have one:
"last read on day X" has no search operator at all, and the progress ladder's `unread` rung
means "never *opened*" (its own `is_read`) while the search's `read:`/`is:unread` filters key
on the `progress` field alone — so they disagree about an archive that was opened without a
page turn. Deriving the list from the same classification the chart used is what keeps the
list and the bar consistent by construction.

Requesting this as a guest is scoped to what that guest may see, matching `/stats/overview`.

parameters.description: `ingest`/`read` only. Last day of the bucket, `YYYY-MM-DD`, inclusive.

parameters.name: key

history (per-day, progress distribution, ratings, and the most recently/most often read
works), and a weighted reading-preference analysis over tags, authors and categories.

Requesting this as a guest yields counts and breakdowns restricted to what that guest may
actually see, matching `/database/stats`'s own scoping.

Weighted preference values are relative rankings, not probabilities or percentages: they are
only ever meaningful against each other within one response.

get.description:
The page's time-series source, kept separate from `/stats/overview` because it is driven
interactively: the overview is one expensive snapshot (its preference analysis runs a search
per dynamic category), while this endpoint is refetched per range change and re-bucketed
entirely client-side.

The series is **always daily**, whatever granularity the reader is looking at, so that
changing granularity — or zooming and panning — needs no request at all once the range has
been fetched once. A request wider than the server's own cap is clamped to the *newest* days
of it, and `available_from` still reports where the data really begins.

Requesting this as a guest is scoped to what that guest may see, matching `/stats/overview`.

Deliberately works on a **disabled** subscription: "what would this rule actually catch" is asked
precisely while tuning one that is switched off. Nothing is queued, recorded as seen, or logged,
